selection.reviewer_identity: storyboard-critic leaf, claude-opus-5-5 high effort, independent exact-muted-phone reviewer (this assignment)
selection.reason: The two films share about 85 percent of their pixels: identical pad opening (0 to 6.2 s), software panel (6.2 to 11.4 s), drone route and infrared inset (22.0 to 26.2 s), inspector review (26.4 to 33.4 s), protocol detail, program and proposal scenes. Where they differ, a keeps the evidence direct and source-faithful. In s3 (11.6 to 19.6 s) the approval letter is stamped with no person present, so muted viewers see EPA's record rather than a reviewer approving. The hero passage starts on the pad itself (19.8 to 22.0 s) with the drone in frame, instead of a tiny drone icon on a wall screen. In s9 the close shot holds the stylus on the green check next to a pad window card (49.0 to 51.2 s), then shows the empty AI box drawn on the review monitor (51.8 to 53.8 s).
selection.rejected_reason: In b the generic inspector is placed in record scenes where the source gives her no role. At 11.6 to 13.8 s the EPA approval letter slides onto her desk, and from 16.8 to 19.6 s she raises a pen toward the letter while the Approved mark lands. Muted, this reads as the reviewer receiving or approving EPA's decision. From 19.8 to 21.6 s, during 'The drone carries an infrared camera', the drone is a tiny icon on a wall-mounted feed screen and the camera is not legible. The inspector sits idle facing right, and watching the live feed implies real-time review, while the letter describes review after the data are collected. She is also held in an unchanging pose at 11.6 to 13.8, 19.8 to 21.6 and 33.6 to 35.6 s. B's ending is stronger: the large empty AI box and pad window card are fully readable from 53.8 to 56.2 s. That alone does not outweigh the implied-role and hero-legibility costs.

report.reviewer_identity: storyboard-critic leaf, claude-opus-5-5 high effort, independent exact-muted-phone reviewer (this assignment)
report.strongest_frame: s5 29.0 to 32.6 s: the inspector's raised stylus traces a dashed outline around the shimmer on the survey footage, presses a green check, then pulls a 'Follow-up inspection' tag off the check and lands it on the round valve inset. Input, human judgement and consequence all happen in one continuous close action.
report.weakest_frame: s9 54.0 to 56.2 s: a static wide room shot ends the story. The empty 'AI' box and the confirmed footage shrink to a few phone pixels, and the drone station through the window is only faintly visible, so the final image restates the answer at its smallest legible size (the box was readable in medium at 52.0 to 53.8 s).

Surface finish was judged at phone size only. Drone, dock, tanks, valves and inspector read as finished flat-vector forms with soft contact shadows. The office set, letters (placeholder grey lines) and monitors are plain. Native-crop finish is unverified here and remains for the native hero review.
Muted review only; sound and caption alignment were not assessed. This review used sampled images, so motion smoothness between samples is unresolved.

dominant_action.observed: The focal subjects perform the narrated changes. The drone tilts and travels along the dashed route into a point-of-interest ring that brightens (22.6 to 23.4 s), and an infrared inset opens from it (24.8 to 25.8 s). The inspector herself outlines, confirms and sends the follow-up tag. None of this is carried by labels or camera drift.

Cuts carry the map-tile drone icon (7.0 s), the approval letter (11.6 s), and the infrared valve from the drone inset to the review footage (26.4 to 27.6 s). The empty dashed 'AI' box then draws on the review monitor and stays empty (51.8 to 53.8 s), and a wide shows the seated inspector, check and box (54.0 to 56.0 s). finished_art.observed: The edition's own drone, dock and pad hero performs lift-off and the route. Support art (panel, letter, stamps, review monitor, valve inset, calendars, tags, AI box) is used for every record. No library boxes stand in for the machinery. Phone-size finish is consistent; plain interiors and placeholder text lines are the weakest surfaces, and native finish was not seen.

story_review.one_viewing_summary: A generic drone leaves its station on a Permian pad. A software panel shows an anomaly flag that the companies, not EPA, claim. EPA's dated letter approves the method. The drone flies its route and an illustrative infrared view opens. A certified inspector outlines and confirms the emission and sends a follow-up tag to the valve. The letter names AI once, in a protocol title, and a separate leak reporting program is delayed and proposed for rescission. The close leaves the inspector's check beside an empty AI box.
story_review.opening_to_ending: The opening asks what a drone over oil equipment does and who calls a leak. The ending answers in picture: the person's green check on the outlined emission, beside an AI box that stays empty. No repair, leak count or outcome is implied.
story_review.weakest_transition: s3 to s4 at 19.6 to 19.8 s: a hard cut from the static approved letter to a wide pad with a small hovering drone. The planned visual link (approved mark becoming the drone) is not visible, so the causal link from approved method to drone performing it relies on narration.

report.phone_decision_scope_applied: Judged against the fixed rubric and quality contract only. The director's promised techniques (camera-pod swing, the station seen through the window at the close, the stamp dissolving into the drone) were not visibly executed. They were treated as notes, not hard requirements, because the picture still meets the fixed criteria.
